newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Petron Corp's new refinery to meet domestic demand.
newsitem.headline: Petron Corp's new refinery to meet domestic demand.

text.p: A senior official of Philippines Petron Corp said on Wednesday its new US$1.4 billion refinery to be completed by 2001 will cater for booming domestic demand.
Alfred Trio, engineering manager of Bataan refinery, told a conference in Singapore the 100-200,000 barrels per day (bpd) refinery would be fully owned by Petron.
It might be located in the Visayas, Mindanao in southern Philippines or Bataan on Luzon Island in the north, he said.

"Domestic demand for petroleum in the Philippines is projected to grow at an annual rate of 5.9 percent," Trio said. "Demand for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) will be growing the fastest at 9.2 percent and motor gasoline at 7.8 percent."
"Petron is now doing a site-selection study for the said grassroots refinery," he told a downstream conference in Singapore.
Trio was speaking a day after Petron announced its board had approved 1997 capital spending plans of 5.374 billion pesos.
Trio said among other plans, Petron also alloted US$436 million to expand its 165,000 bpd Bataan refinery in three tranches.
The first, which is already in full swing, includes debottlenecking crude distillation unit number two at Bataan, adding 15,000 bpd output capacity to 180,000 bpd.
The debottleknecking is expected to cost $43 million and should be complete by early 1998, Trio said.
The units would cater for a projected shift in demand from fuel oil to lighter products like LPG, gasoline and diesel and help reduce the sulphur content of fuel oil and diesel.
He said Petron was also considering building a power generator to provide power for the planned units.
Trio told Reuters that longer term the refinery was also considering petrochemicals as another outlet, but he declined to elaborate.
Petron is 40 percent owned by Philippine National Oil Company (PNOC) and 40 percent by Saudi ARAMCO. The remaining 20 percent is owned by the public.

The second tranche, which will cost $160 million, is to install a 17,000 bpd continuous catalyst regeneration reformer unit (CCR), the installation of a 70 tons-per-day sulphur recovery unit (SRU) and the installation of various support units like steam and power generators.
The CCR will address Philippines move to unleaded gasoline, scheduled by the year 2,000. The SRU cuts back sulphur in gases.
Petron's third tranche covered the feasibility of installing a mild hydrocracker and delayed coker unit. If the tranche goes ahead it would cost $233 million, Trio said.
